newsitem.title: USA: Sun to restructure Puerto Rican refinery.
newsitem.headline: Sun to restructure Puerto Rican refinery.

text.p: Sun Co Inc said Tuesday it will restructure its refinery in Yabucoa, P.R., to improve its efficiency and profitability.
The company said the major change will be to switch from processing crude oil as a feedstock to processing purchased intermediate feedstocks such as vacuum gas oil and reduced crude.

Sun Lubricants Vice President Bill Thompson said the change in feedstock will eliminate much of the refinery's fuels production and allow it to focus on production of the profitable lubricant base oils.
"The changes will be made during the first quarter of 1997, and they will make the refinery more competitive and significantly improve its profitability," he said.

The refinery, which is part of Sun's Lubricants business unit, currently processes 75,000 barrels a day of crude oil, the company said. Sun operates it principally to produce lubricant base oils, but in its current configuration the facility also produces over 50,000 barrels per day of fuels.
In recent years, weak fuels products margins, especially for residual fuel, have reduced overall profitability, Sun pointed out.

"Following the restructuring, the refinery will process between 20,000 and 30,000 barrels a day of intermediate feedstock, but the volume and quality of the lubricant base oil production will not be affected," Thompson said.
Recent capital improvements have increased the production capacity of Yabucoa's high quality, hydrotreated base oils to over 9,000 barrels per day.

Thompson said that some of the processing units in the refinery would be shut down as a part of the change. These include the atmospheric crude tower, the gasoline reformer, and the gas oil desulfurizer.
He said more than 75 jobs would be eliminated as a result of these closings and related efficiency improvements. The plant currently employs 340 people.
The fuels now produced at the refinery -- gasoline, jet fuel, distillate fuel, and residual fuel -- are sold on-island.

"We will meet out obligations under our current contracts with fuels customers utilizing products we acquire elsewhere," Thompson said, "and we hope to maintain our on-island marketing presence in the future."
